syllabus.clause: reading the database's own replication log (complete, ordered, low overhead, but operationally coupled to the source)

at.step: Reveal: write cost and log cost, both measured

items.item: Logical decoding is the process of extracting all persistent changes to a database's tables into a coherent, easy to understand format
PostgreSQL normally purges write-ahead log (WAL) segments after some period of time, so the connector does not have the complete history of all changes

A poll's own query sees only the state of a row at the moment it runs, measured directly: four real statements (one insert, three status updates) against a test order, read back by a single poll query, show only the final status.

A real logical replication slot, decoding the identical window with the test_decoding plugin, returns every one of the four states in the exact commit order they happened, which is what the poll's own single sample structurally cannot do.

A poll's watermark query cannot distinguish a row that never existed from one that existed and was deleted inside the same interval, measured directly: an inserted-then-deleted test row returns zero matches from the poll's own query, identical to a row that was never inserted at all.
The identical deleted row's own delete event is present, named and ordered, in the replication slot's own decoded output, measured directly as exactly one DELETE event for that row's id.

A trigger-based shadow table doubles every write it captures, measured directly: four real writes to a test order through a real AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE trigger produce exactly four corresponding rows in the shadow table, a one-to-one, not partial, amplification.

at.step: Reveal: write cost and log cost, both measured

items.item: A logical replication slot's own read cost scales with the number of real changes made, not with the size of the table being watched, measured directly: three real changes against a table of over fifty thousand rows return exactly three change events from the slot.

at.step: Reveal: write cost and log cost, both measured

items.item: The wrong half of the first predict question — that a trigger only fires on a transaction's final state — is ruled out by PostgreSQL's own trigger semantics and by direct measurement: an AFTER UPDATE trigger fires once per row-affecting statement, inside that statement's own transaction.

items.item: The wrong half of the final predict question — that reading WAL is entirely free — is ruled out by the Debezium quote directly: WAL is purged after a retention window, so a consumer's own position in that log is a real, ongoing cost, not a free lunch.
